Each card is { id, category, front, back }. `id` is the STABLE scheduling key — never reuse or renumber an id once cards have been reviewed, or a card's saved schedule will attach to the wrong prompt. To grow the deck, append new cards with fresh ids; order here is only the tie-break order in which brand-new cards are introduced. Categories in use: Positions, Preflop, Math, Board Texture, Hand Rankings, Bankroll.

cards.back: Under the Gun — the seat first to act preflop, immediately left of the big blind. It acts with the least information, so it plays the tightest range.
Cutoff — the seat directly to the right of the button. A late position and the second-best seat, so it opens a wide range of hands.
Button — the dealer seat. The best position at the table: it acts last on every postflop street, so it plays the widest range.
Small blind and big blind — the two seats left of the button forced to post bets before cards are dealt. They act last preflop but first postflop, which makes them awkward to play.

cards.front: What does it mean to be "in position" (IP)?
cards.back: You act after your opponent on every postflop street — you see what they do before you decide. That information edge is a large, persistent advantage.
You act before your opponent postflop, giving away information first. You need a stronger range to play profitably out of position.

cards.front: Why is the Button the most profitable seat?
cards.back: Because it always acts last postflop — maximum information on every street — so you can play more hands and value-bet or bluff more accurately.

cards.front: Name the 6-max positions in order of action.
cards.back: UTG, MP (a.k.a. LoJack/HiJack), CO, BTN, SB, BB. Action moves clockwise; the earlier the seat, the tighter it should play.
Raise First In — you are the first player to voluntarily enter the pot, and you do it by raising rather than calling. Open-raising, not limping, is the standard.

cards.front: Why does your position set your opening range?
cards.back: Later positions have fewer players left to act and act last postflop, so they can profitably open many more hands. Early position must stay tight.
The first voluntary raise into a pot no one has entered yet. A standard size is about 2–3 big blinds (often 2.5bb online).
The third bet in a preflop sequence: the big blind is bet 1, an open-raise is bet 2, and a re-raise over that is the 3-bet. Made with strong value hands and some bluffs.

cards.front: Why raise instead of limp (just calling the big blind)?
cards.back: Raising builds the pot with your good hands, seizes the initiative, and can win the pot immediately when everyone folds. Limping surrenders all of that.
Voluntarily Put money In Pot — the percentage of hands you choose to play. A core tightness stat; solid 6-max regulars sit around 20–25%.
The price of a call: the amount you must call relative to the total pot after you call. They tell you the minimum equity your hand needs to call profitably.

cards.front: How do you turn pot odds into a required equity %?
cards.back: Required equity = (amount to call) ÷ (pot size after your call). Example: call 50 into a pot that becomes 200 → 50/200 = 25% equity needed.
A card still in the deck that improves your hand to a likely winner. Counting your outs is how you estimate your chance to improve.

cards.front: How many outs does a flush draw have?
cards.back: 9. You hold two of a suit and two are on the board; nine of the remaining thirteen cards of that suit complete the flush.

cards.front: How many outs does an open-ended straight draw have?
cards.back: 8. Either of two ranks completes the straight, and there are four cards of each rank (4 + 4 = 8).

cards.front: How many outs does a gutshot (inside straight draw) have?
cards.back: 4. Only one rank fills the gap in the middle of the straight, and there are four cards of that rank.
A quick equity estimate: multiply your outs by 2 for one card to come, or by 4 for two cards (flop through river). E.g. a 9-out flush draw ≈ 18% on the turn, ≈ 36% by the river.

cards.front: With a flush draw on the flop, roughly what is your equity by the river?
cards.back: About 36% (9 outs × 4). So against a single bet you can often call profitably when the pot is laying you better than roughly 2-to-1.

cards.front: Why compare your equity to the pot odds?
cards.back: If your hand's equity is greater than the equity the pot odds demand, calling is profitable in the long run. That single comparison is the whole call/fold decision.
A disconnected board with few draws (e.g. K♠ 7♦ 2♣). Few hands connect with it, so the preflop raiser can bet small and often.
A connected and/or suited board offering many straight and flush draws (e.g. 9♥ 8♥ 6♠). Ranges collide, so bets tend to be larger to charge those draws.
A board that itself contains a pair (e.g. Q♣ Q♦ 4♠). It lowers the chance anyone holds trips and changes which full houses and quads are possible.
A flop of three cards of the same suit (e.g. J♠ 8♠ 3♠). Anyone with one card of that suit has a flush draw, and a made flush is already possible.

cards.front: Why does board texture affect your bet sizing?
cards.back: On dry boards few hands can continue, so small bets do the job; on wet boards you charge draws and protect your equity with larger bets. Texture drives the size.
A board with cards close in rank (e.g. 7 8 9) that makes straights likely. It favors the range holding more suited connectors and small pairs.

cards.front: List the poker hands from weakest to strongest.
cards.back: High card, pair, two pair, three of a kind, straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, straight flush (royal flush is the top straight flush).

cards.front: Does a flush beat a straight?
cards.back: Yes. A flush (five cards of one suit) beats a straight (five in sequence). A full house then beats the flush.

cards.front: Rank these from best to worst: flush, straight, full house.
cards.back: Full house > flush > straight. The full house beats the flush, which beats the straight.
A flush, a full house, four of a kind, and a straight flush — in that ascending order.

cards.front: Which is stronger: two pair or three of a kind?
cards.back: Three of a kind (a set or trips) beats two pair.
The best possible hand on a given board. If you hold the nuts, no opponent's hand can beat you at that moment.

cards.front: How many buy-ins should a cash-game bankroll be?
cards.back: At least 20–30+ buy-ins for the stake you play, so normal downswings can't bust you. Example: 30 × $200 = a $6,000 roll for $1/$2.
Poker has heavy short-term variance. A deep enough roll lets your long-term edge play out without going broke during an inevitable downswing.
Playing stakes small enough relative to your money that variance can't ruin you — and moving down when your roll shrinks. It's discipline, not ego.

cards.front: Should your poker bankroll be money you need for living expenses?
cards.back: No. A bankroll is dedicated risk capital, kept separate from rent and bills. Only ever play with money you can afford to lose.
